## 1. Introduction and Study Context

Urban Rail Transit (URT) is central to sustainable urban development. By moving large numbers of people quickly and reliably, it supports transit-oriented development, reduces road congestion and connects residents to jobs, services and education. In Singapore, the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) system has been the backbone of public transport since 1987. Today it has six lines, more than 140 stations and about 200 km of track, complemented by two Light Rail Transit (LRT) lines of about 28 km (Land Transport Authority [LTA], n.d.). In 2024, the MRT carried an average of 3.41 million rides a day, exceeding pre-pandemic levels for the first time (“Singapore’s MRT, LRT ridership surpasses pre-Covid-19 levels”, 2025).

Expanding the network carries a planning risk. Stations are often built ahead of demand to avoid future disruption and cost, but a station that opens before its catchment has developed incurs operating costs with few riders. Hume station’s structure was built as part of Downtown Line Stage 2, which opened in 2015, but the station was left unfinished because its projected ridership did not justify full construction (“Hume MRT station”, n.d.). It opened only on 28 February 2025 (LTA, 2025). Similarly, Buangkok and Woodleigh stations remained closed when the North East Line opened in 2003, because the areas around them were not yet developed enough to justify their operating costs. They opened in 2006 and 2011 respectively (“Buangkok MRT station”, n.d.; “Woodleigh MRT station”, n.d.). Such decisions depend on estimating a station's catchment and predicting its ridership before it opens.

Two new lines will add 36 stations by 2030: the Jurong Region Line (JRL, 24 stations) and Phase 1 of the Cross Island Line (CRL, 12 stations). New stations also compete with existing ones. Residents who live between an existing and a new station may switch, so the new lines can reduce ridership at existing stations as well as add their own.

Probabilistic spatial interaction models address this question directly. The Huff model estimates the probability that a resident at a given location uses each station, based on the station's attractiveness and the distance to it, relative to all competing stations (Huff, 1964). Zhu et al. (2021) applied an improved Huff model to estimate URT station catchments in Xi'an, measuring station attractiveness through walkability, public transport accessibility and service quality. However, they adopted the distance-decay and attractiveness parameters from the literature and from expert ratings rather than calibrating them, and noted this as their main limitation. This exercise calibrates the model parameters against observed station ridership in Singapore, using the Multiplicative Competitive Interaction (MCI) model, the calibratable form of the Huff model (Nakanishi & Cooper, 1974).

Please refer to the [Executive Summary](https://kay-geohub.vercel.app/Take-Home_Ex/Take-Home_Ex03/Take-Home_Ex03_ExSum.html#/title-slide) for the key analysis and recommendations.

## 2. Research Objectives and Questions

### 2.1 Research Objectives

This exercise develops an analytical framework for station-level ridership prediction to:

- Calibrate a probabilistic spatial interaction model for station-level ridership estimation.
- Predict the potential ridership of the proposed JRL and CRL Phase 1 stations.
- Evaluate the potential impact of the new stations on the ridership and market areas of existing stations.

### 2.2 Research Questions

- **RQ1:** How well does a calibrated probabilistic spatial interaction model explain the observed weekday morning-peak ridership of existing MRT and LRT stations, and which station attributes matter beyond distance?
- **RQ2:** What ridership can be expected at the 36 proposed JRL and CRL Phase 1 stations, and which stations are at risk of low ridership?
- **RQ3:** How will the new stations redistribute the market areas and ridership of existing stations?

### 2.3 Model Components

| Component | Definition in this exercise | Data |
|--------------------|--------------------------------|--------------------|
| Origins | Hexagonal grid cells covering mainland Singapore | Created in this exercise |
| Market potential | Residents aged 15-64 in HDB and private housing, June 2026 | SingStat population by subzone, HDB Property Information, HDB Existing Building, MP2019 Land Use |
| Destinations | Existing MRT/LRT stations, and existing plus proposed stations | LTA Train Station, URA Master Plan 2025 Rail Station |
| Observed ridership | Average weekday tap-ins between 7am and 9am, July-September 2026 | LTA Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Train Stations |
| Attractiveness | Candidate station attributes, such as nearby points of interest, bus interchanges and bus stops, the number of lines served, and station type (MRT or LRT) | OpenStreetMap, LTA Bus Stop |
| Distance | Straight-line distance from each hexagon to each station, in metres | Computed in this exercise |

Market potential is defined as HDB residents aged 15 to 64, covering the secondary-school, tertiary and working-age groups that make up most weekday morning-peak MRT trips. Children under 15 are excluded because most travel to nearby primary schools on foot or by school bus. Residents aged 65 and over are excluded because their trips are less concentrated in the morning peak.

### 3.4 Downloading the Passenger Volume Data

Unlike the other datasets, the passenger volume data cannot be downloaded directly from a web page. It is served through the LTA DataMall API, which requires an Account Key. To reproduce this step, request an Account Key at the [LTA DataMall API request page](https://datamall.lta.gov.sg/content/datamall/en/request-for-api.html). The key is sent by email.

DataMall only provides the three most recent months. The July to September 2026 files will therefore no longer be available from the API after December 2026.

The key is stored in a `.Renviron` file in the project folder as `LTA_ACCOUNT_KEY=<your key>`, and read with *Sys.getenv()*, so it never appears in the report or on GitHub. `.Renviron` is listed in `.gitignore`. The chunk is set to `eval: false` because the API only serves the three most recent months.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
for (m in c("202607", "202608", "202609")) {
  resp <- request("https://datamall2.mytransport.sg/ltaodataservice/PV/ODTrain") %>%
    req_url_query(Date = m) %>%
    req_headers(AccountKey = Sys.getenv("LTA_ACCOUNT_KEY"),
                accept     = "application/json") %>%
    req_perform()

  zip_link <- resp_body_json(resp)$value[[1]]$Link   
  zip_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
  download.file(zip_link, zip_file, mode = "wb")
  unzip(zip_file, exdir = "data/aspatial")          
}
```
:::


### 3.5 Importing Geospatial Data

The eight geospatial datasets are imported with *st_read()*. GeoJSON files are read by file path. Shapefiles are read by folder (`dsn`) and layer name, because a shapefile consists of several files (`.shp`, `.shx`, `.dbf`, `.prj`) that must sit together in the same folder.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mpsz_raw     <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaGEOJSON.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
landuse_raw  <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019LandUselayer.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
hdb_bldg_raw <- st_read("data/geospatial/HDBExistingBuilding.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
mp25_stn_raw <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2025RailStationLayer.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
rts_raw      <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial/RapidTransitSystemStation", layer = "RapidTransitSystemStation", quiet = TRUE)
busstop_raw  <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial/BusStopLocation_Sep2026", layer = "BusStop", quiet = TRUE)
poi_pt_raw   <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial/gis_osm_pois", layer = "gis_osm_pois_free_1", quiet = TRUE)
poi_poly_raw <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial/gis_osm_pois", layer = "gis_osm_pois_a_free_1", quiet = TRUE)
```
:::


To check all eight layers at once, the code chunk below summarises each layer’s number of features, geometry type, coordinate reference system (CRS) and number of invalid geometries.

AI tools were used to draft the R code that summarises the eight layers into a single table using *imap()* and *list_rbind()*. The output was reviewed and run by the author to verify correctness against the study data.

The summary shows three issues that are addressed in Section 4:

- **Mixed coordinate systems.** The GeoJSON files and the OpenStreetMap files are in WGS 84 (longitude and latitude, in degrees), while the two LTA shapefiles are in SVY21 without an EPSG code. Distances must be measured in metres, so all layers are projected to SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414).
- **Invalid geometries.** A small number of polygons are invalid, for example with self-intersecting outlines: 6 in the subzone boundary, 3 in the land use layer and 4 in the HDB building layer. These can cause spatial joins and overlays to fail or return wrong results.
- **OpenStreetMap coverage.** The extract covers Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei, so 108,841 points and 64,468 polygons are imported, most of them outside Singapore. They are clipped to the study area when station attractiveness is prepared.

## 4. Data Wrangling

### 4.1 CRS Transformation and Geometry Repair

All layers are projected to SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414), Singapore's national projected coordinate system, which measures distance in metres.

The two LTA shapefiles are already in SVY21 coordinates, but their projection file does not carry the EPSG code. Either *st_set_crs()* (which relabels the CRS without changing the coordinates) or *st_transform()* (which converts the coordinates) could be used. Before choosing, the two results were compared:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
max(abs(st_coordinates(st_set_crs(rts_raw, 3414))[, 1:2] -
        st_coordinates(st_transform(rts_raw, 3414))[, 1:2]))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0
```


:::
:::


The largest difference is 0 m, confirming that the shapefiles' SVY21 definition is identical to EPSG:3414. *st_transform()* is therefore used for every layer.

Invalid geometries in the land use and HDB building layers are repaired with *st_make_valid()*. The subzone boundary is processed separately in Section 4.2.

The subzone boundary is used both to define the study area and to link the SingStat population data to locations, so its subzone names must match the population table exactly.

data.gov.sg has distributed this file in two formats. In one, the attributes are ordinary columns (`SUBZONE_N`, `PLN_AREA_N` and so on). In the other, all attributes are packed into an HTML table in a single `Description` column. *names()* shows which format was downloaded:


::: {.cell}

```
 [6] "PLN_AREA_N" "PLN_AREA_C" "REGION_N"   "REGION_C"   "INC_CRC"   
[11] "FMEL_UPD_D" "SHAPE.AREA" "SHAPE.LEN"  "geometry"
```

:::
:::


If the attributes sit inside `Description`, the code below extracts each one with a regular expression, which captures the text between `<th>FIELD</th><td>` and `</td>`. If they are already columns, this step is skipped.

::: callout-note
### AI Use Disclosure

AI tools were used to draft the regular expression that extracts subzone attributes from the HTML in the `Description` column. The output was reviewed and run by the author to verify correctness against the study data.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
if (!"SUBZONE_N" %in% names(mpsz_raw)) {
  get_attr <- function(html, field) {
    str_match(html, paste0("<th>", field, "</th>\\s*<td>(.*?)</td>"))[, 2]
  }
  for (field in c("SUBZONE_N", "SUBZONE_C", "PLN_AREA_N",
                  "PLN_AREA_C", "REGION_N", "REGION_C")) {
    mpsz_raw[[field]] <- get_attr(mpsz_raw$Description, field)
  }
}
```
:::


The boundary is then cleaned:

- *select()* keeps the subzone, planning area and region names and codes.
- *st_transform()* projects to EPSG:3414, and *st_make_valid()* then repairs invalid polygons.

### 4.3 Preparing the Study Boundary

The study area is mainland Singapore. Offshore islands are excluded because they have no HDB flats and no MRT or LRT stations, and therefore neither market potential nor destinations.

Excluding islands needs care. Jurong Island and Sentosa are joined to the mainland by causeways, so in the boundary file their polygons touch the mainland. Keeping only the largest piece of land would therefore still include them. Instead, the study area is built in three steps:

1.  The three planning areas that consist of offshore islands are removed: Western Islands (including Jurong Island), Southern Islands (including Sentosa) and North-Eastern Islands (Pulau Ubin and Pulau Tekong).

2.  The remaining subzones are merged with *st_union()* and split into separate pieces of land with *st_cast("POLYGON")*. The largest piece is mainland Singapore. Smaller islands that belong to mainland planning areas, such as Pulau Seletar, are dropped at this step.

3.  Merging adjacent subzones can leave small gaps along shared borders, which appear as holes in the merged polygon. These are slivers rather than real features, so the holes are filled by keeping only the polygon's outer ring.


::: {.cell}

### 4.7 Preparing the Market Potential

The market potential of each hexagon is the number of residents aged 15 to 64 who live in it. SingStat publishes population only by subzone, so residents are spread within each subzone to where they actually live:

- **HDB residents** are spread across HDB residential blocks in proportion to the number of flats in each block.
- **Residents of private housing** (condominiums, landed homes and other non-HDB dwellings) are spread across private residential land parcels in proportion to each parcel's land area.

Spreading population this way, rather than evenly across a subzone's area, is known as dasymetric mapping: population is removed from uninhabited areas and reassigned to the areas where people live (Eicher & Brewer, 2001; Mennis, 2003). It prevents residents from being placed in parks, industrial estates or reservoirs that share a subzone with housing.

No population values are created or estimated in this process. Each subzone's residents are taken exactly from SingStat, and only their location within the subzone is determined.

#### 4.7.1 Residents aged 15 to 64 by subzone

The SingStat table gives residents for every combination of subzone, age group and type of dwelling. Two dwelling-type rows are used:

- **`Total`**: all residents of the subzone, in every type of dwelling.
- **`Total HDB^`**: residents of HDB flats of all sizes. The footnote to the table states that this also includes non-privatised Housing and Urban Development Company flats.

SingStat does not publish a separate total for private housing. Private-housing residents are therefore obtained by subtraction:

$$
\text{private residents} = \text{Total} - \text{Total HDB}
$$

This covers condominiums and other apartments, landed properties and other types of dwelling, which together make up every resident not living in an HDB flat.

For each subzone, the table is filtered to the ten five-year age groups from `15 - 19` to `60 - 64` and to the two dwelling-type rows, and the population is summed. *pivot_wider()* then places the two totals side by side so that the subtraction can be done row by row.

Two details of the SingStat data are handled explicitly:

- **`-` values.** The table footnote defines `-` as nil or negligible. These were read as missing in Section 3.6.4, and are set to 0 here in line with that definition.
- **Rounding.** SingStat rounds each figure to the nearest 10. In a subzone with almost no private housing, the rounded total can be slightly smaller than the rounded HDB figure, which would give a small negative count. *pmax()* sets any such value to 0.


::: {.cell}

#### 4.7.2 Locating HDB residential blocks

HDB Property Information records whether each block is residential and how many flats it has, but not where it is. The HDB Existing Building layer has each block's location, but not its flat count. The two must be joined, but they share no common identifier:

- Property Information identifies a block by `blk_no` and an abbreviated street name, such as `TOH GUAN RD`.
- The building layer identifies a block by `BLK_NO` and a street code, such as `TOG02Q`.

Block numbers repeat across streets, so `blk_no` alone is not enough. Geocoding each block's address through an online service would need about 10,800 requests, and the report would then depend on that service being available. Instead, the street codes are linked to street names from the data themselves. The idea is that a street code and a street name that refer to the same street should list largely the same set of block numbers.

The matching proceeds as follows:

1. Every building is paired with every property record that has the same block number.
2. For each street code and street name pair, `shared_blocks` counts how many block numbers they have in common. A true pair, such as `TOG02Q` and `TOH GUAN RD`, shares many blocks. A false pair usually shares only one.
3. Pairs are ranked by `shared_blocks`. Ties are broken by whether the street code and street name begin with the same two letters (`TO`), since street codes are formed from the street name.
4. Each building is assigned to its best-ranked property record, and each property record to its best-ranked building, so that no block is used twice. Any building or record that loses its best match to a stronger pair is matched again among the remaining candidates. This repeats until no further matches can be made.

#### 4.7.4 Allocating private-housing residents to land parcels

Private-housing residents are placed using the Master Plan 2019 land use layer, in three steps.

**Step 1: identify private residential land.** Four land-use types are treated as residential: `RESIDENTIAL`, `RESIDENTIAL WITH COMMERCIAL AT 1ST STOREY`, `COMMERCIAL & RESIDENTIAL` and `RESIDENTIAL / INSTITUTION`. HDB estates are also zoned residential, so any parcel that contains an HDB building is removed. The remaining parcels are private housing.

**Step 2: weight each parcel by its land area.** Within each subzone, private-housing residents are spread across these parcels in proportion to land area. This is the areametric approach of Lwin and Murayama (2009), which needs no information on building height or floor area. A weighting by floor area, using each parcel's gross plot ratio (`GPR`), was considered but not used. Most private residential parcels are landed housing (`LND`) or carry codes with no numeric plot ratio, so it would require assumed values. Land area is measured for every parcel, so no values need to be assumed.

**Step 3: share each subzone's residents among its parcels.** Each parcel is represented by a point with *st_point_on_surface()* and assigned to its subzone with *st_join()*. A parcel's residents are its share of the subzone's private residential land multiplied by the subzone's private-housing residents from Section 4.7.1:

$$
\text{residents}_p = \frac{\text{land area}_p}{\sum_{q \in s} \text{land area}_q} \times \text{private residents}_s
$$

Where parcel $p$ lies in subzone $s$. The shares within each subzone sum to 1, so each subzone's total matches SingStat exactly.

The weighting only affects where residents are placed within a subzone. Its main limitation is that a condominium receives the same weight per square metre as landed housing, although it houses more people. Large residential parcels that are not yet fully developed also receive a share in proportion to their size. As each subzone's total is fixed, these effects are confined to a single subzone and mostly to neighbouring 500 m hexagons.

### 4.8 Creating the Hexagon Grid

#### 4.8.1 Hexagon size

Hexagons are used rather than squares because every neighbour of a hexagon is the same distance from its centre, and a hexagon is closer to a circle, so distances measured from its centre represent all of its area more evenly.

*st_make_grid()* with `square = FALSE` creates hexagons, and `cellsize` sets the distance between opposite sides. A cellsize of 500 m is used, giving hexagons of about 0.22 km², with every point within about 290 m of the centre. This size is chosen because:

- **It is finer than station spacing.** Neighbouring stations are typically about 1km apart, so each station's catchment spans several hexagons. The model can therefore show residents splitting between nearby competing stations.
- **It matches walking distance.** A 400 m walking catchment covers about two to three hexagons.
- **It keeps the model manageable.** The number of populated hexagons multiplied by 213 stations gives a few hundred thousand origin-destination pairs.

Results can depend on the size of the areal units used (the modifiable areal unit problem). This is noted as a limitation.

#### 4.8.2 Building the grid and summing population

The grid is generated over the study area's bounding box, and only hexagons that touch the study area are kept with *st_filter()*. Hexagons along the coast are then clipped to land with *st_intersection()*, so that each hexagon's representative point lies on land. Each population point is assigned to the hexagon it falls in, and residents are summed per hexagon.

### 4.9 Preparing the Attractiveness Variables

In the Huff and MCI models, a station's attractiveness is what draws residents to it ahead of a nearer station. Following Zhu et al. (2021), who measured attractiveness through the surrounding built environment, public transport access and the service a station offers, the candidate variables below are built from the data available for Singapore:

| Variable | Definition | Concept (Zhu et al., 2021) |
|------------------|-------------------------------|-------------------------|
| `n_lines` | Number of MRT/LRT lines serving the station | Service quality |
| `bus_stops` | Bus stops within 400 m | Public transport access |
| `bus_int` | Whether a bus interchange lies within 400 m | Public transport access |
| `shopping` | Malls, department stores, supermarkets and markets within 400 m | Built environment |
| `food` | Food courts, restaurants, fast-food outlets and cafés within 400 m | Built environment |
| `education` | Schools, colleges and universities within 400 m | Built environment |
| `healthcare` | Hospitals, clinics and doctors within 400 m | Built environment |
| `community` | Community centres, libraries and sports centres within 400 m | Built environment |

A radius of 400 m, about a five-minute walk, is used to capture what lies immediately around each station. Which of these variables are kept in the final model is decided during calibration (Section 5), taking into account their correlation, shown in Section 4.9.4.

### 4.10 Building the Spatial Interaction Data Frames

#### 4.10.1 Distance matrices

The distance from every origin to every station is computed with *st_distance()*. Origins are passed first and stations second, so that each row of the matrix is an origin and each column a station. The row and column names are set to `hex_id` and `station` before the matrix is converted to long format with *pivot_longer()*, so each distance stays attached to the correct origin and station. Each origin's point lies inside its hexagon, as prepared in Section 4.8.2.

The same steps are applied to the existing and future networks, so they are wrapped in a function. The function also attaches each station's attractiveness variables, giving one row per origin-station pair. The columns are ordered with origin first, station second, then distance and attractiveness, which is the long format the MCI functions require.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
build_si <- function(origins, dest) {
  dmat <- st_distance(origins, dest)
  rownames(dmat) <- origins$hex_id
  colnames(dmat) <- dest$station

  dmat %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column("hex_id") %>%
    pivot_longer(-hex_id, names_to = "station", values_to = "distance") %>%
    mutate(distance = as.numeric(distance)) %>%
    left_join(dest %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(station, all_of(attr_vars)),
              by = "station")
}

si_existing <- build_si(origins, dest_existing)
si_future   <- build_si(origins, dest_future)

c(existing_rows = nrow(si_existing), future_rows = nrow(si_future))
```

## 5. Calibrating the Spatial Interaction Model

### 5.1 Model Specification

The Huff model (Huff, 1964) gives the probability that a resident of hexagon $i$ uses station $j$, relative to all competing stations $k$:

$$
P_{ij} = \frac{A_j \, d_{ij}^{\lambda}}{\sum_{k} A_k \, d_{ik}^{\lambda}}
$$

where $A_j$ is the attractiveness of station $j$, $d_{ij}$ is the distance from hexagon $i$ to station $j$, and $\lambda$ is the distance-decay exponent. $\lambda$ is negative, so a more distant station is less likely to be chosen. The larger its magnitude, the more strongly residents prefer the nearest station.

In the original Huff model, attractiveness is a single variable. The Multiplicative Competitive Interaction (MCI) model (Nakanishi & Cooper, 1974) extends it to several attributes, each raised to its own exponent $\gamma_m$:

$$
A_j = \prod_{m} X_{mj}^{\gamma_m}
$$

A positive $\gamma_m$ means the attribute makes a station more attractive, and the size of $\gamma_m$ shows how strongly.

Predicted morning-peak tap-ins at each station are the probabilities weighted by the trips generated in each hexagon:

$$
\hat{T}_j = \sum_i P_{ij} \, r \, C_i, \qquad r = \frac{\sum_j T_j}{\sum_i C_i}
$$

where $C_i$ is the market potential of hexagon $i$ (residents aged 15-64), $T_j$ is the observed tap-ins at station $j$, and $r$ is the overall trip rate. The trip rate puts market potential and tap-ins on the same scale: without it, predicted totals would sum to the population rather than to the number of tap-ins. This corresponds to *shares.total()* in the **MCI** package, used in Kam (2026, Chapter 18) to estimate store sales from market shares.

#### 5.1.1 Calibrating from station totals

The standard way to calibrate an MCI model is ordinary least squares on log-centred market shares (Nakanishi & Cooper, 1974). It requires observed shares for every origin-destination pair, i.e. how many residents of each hexagon used each station. That information is not available: the passenger volume data record tap-ins by station, not by where riders live.

When only totals per location are known, Huff-type models are instead calibrated by nonlinear fitting. The parameters are adjusted until predicted totals match observed totals as closely as possible (Orpana & Lampinen, 2003; De Beule et al., 2014; Wieland, 2017, 2026). The same approach is used here. $\lambda$ and the MCI exponents $\gamma_m$ are estimated together by minimising the squared difference between the logarithms of predicted and observed tap-ins:

$$
\min_{\lambda,\,\gamma} \; \sum_j \left( \ln \hat{T}_j - \ln T_j \right)^2
$$

Logarithms are used so that the fit is judged on relative rather than absolute error. Otherwise, the dozen busiest stations, with over 10,000 tap-ins each, would dominate the fit, and stations with a few hundred tap-ins would be ignored.

The **MCI** package's *huff.fit()* also fits to totals, but it does so by giving every station its own attractiveness value. That reproduces the existing stations almost perfectly but cannot predict a station that has not yet opened, which is the purpose of this exercise. Estimating exponents for station attributes allows attractiveness to be computed for the new stations from their attributes.

#### 5.1.2 Models compared

Three models are calibrated, each adding one element to the previous one, so that the gain from each element can be assessed:

| Model | Attractiveness $A_j$ | Distance decay $\lambda$ | Purpose |
|------------------|-----------------------|------------------|-------------------------------------|
| **M0: Null Huff** | Equal for all stations | Fixed at -2 | Reference model: distance alone, with the conventional value of $\lambda$ adopted by Zhu et al. (2021) and the default in the **MCI** package |
| **M1: Calibrated Huff** | Equal for all stations | Estimated | Tests whether distance decay in Singapore differs from the conventional value |
| **M2: MCI** | Product of station attributes | Estimated | Tests whether station attributes improve the fit; used for prediction |

#### 5.1.3 Assumptions

- **Residents aged 15-64 generate morning-peak tap-ins at the same rate everywhere** ($r$ is the same for every hexagon).
- **Every resident can choose any station.** As shown in Section 4.10.2, distant stations receive very small probabilities.
- **Straight-line distance represents the effort of reaching a station.** Actual walking routes, feeder bus routes and barriers such as expressways are not modelled.
- **Opening new stations redistributes riders rather than creating new ones.** The total number of tap-ins is held constant when the new stations are added in Section 6.

Two functions implement the model. *huff_prob()* computes $P_{ij}$ for every hexagon and station. It works with the logarithm of each term and subtracts the row maximum before exponentiating, which gives the same probabilities but avoids numerical overflow. *predict_totals()* then computes $\hat{T}_j$. *fit_stats()* summarises how well predicted totals match observed ones:

- **Pseudo-R²:** the squared correlation between predicted and observed tap-ins.
- **R² of logs:** the same on the log scale, which gives small stations equal weight.
- **Median absolute percentage error (median APE):** the typical relative error at a station. The median is used rather than the mean because a few stations with very few tap-ins, such as Teck Lee LRT with about 6, would otherwise dominate.
- **Root mean squared error (RMSE):** the typical error in tap-ins.

### AI Use Disclosure

AI tools were used to draft the vectorised R functions *huff_prob()* and *predict_totals()*, including the numerically stable computation of probabilities using *sweep()*. The output was reviewed by the author and checked against *huff.shares()* and *shares.total()* of the **MCI** package below.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
huff_prob <- function(D, logA, lambda) {
  U <- sweep(lambda * log(D), 2, logA, "+")   # log of A_j * d_ij^lambda
  U <- U - apply(U, 1, max)                    # avoid overflow; probabilities unchanged
  P <- exp(U)
  P / rowSums(P)
}

predict_totals <- function(D, logA, lambda) {
  as.vector(crossprod(huff_prob(D, logA, lambda), C_i * trip_rate))
}

fit_stats <- function(T_hat, T_obs) {
  tibble(pseudo_r2  = cor(T_hat, T_obs)^2,
         r2_log     = cor(log(T_hat), log(T_obs))^2,
         median_ape = median(abs(T_hat - T_obs) / T_obs) * 100,
         rmse       = sqrt(mean((T_hat - T_obs)^2)))
}
```

### 5.5 M2: MCI Model

The MCI model estimates $\lambda$ together with an exponent for each attractiveness variable. All nine variables are entered: the eight prepared in Section 4.9 and mrt. No pair is correlated above 0.8 (Section 4.9.4).

*optim()* with the BFGS method searches for the parameter values that minimise the log error, starting from $\lambda = -2$ and all exponents at 0, i.e. M0. With `hessian = TRUE`, it also returns the curvature of the loss at the solution. From this, approximate standard errors are computed using the standard result for least-squares estimation: the covariance of the estimates is $2\hat{\sigma}^2 H^{-1}$, where $H$ is the Hessian and $\hat{\sigma}^2$ the residual variance. Each estimate is then tested against zero with a z-test.

The fit is wrapped in a function with a `train` argument, so the same code can be reused for the holdout test in Section 5.8.

```{.r .cell-code}
vars_m2 <- c("n_lines", "mrt", "bus_stops", "bus_int",
             "shopping", "food", "education", "healthcare", "community")
X_exist  <- log(as.matrix(dest_df[, vars_m2]))
X_future <- log(as.matrix(dest_future_df[, vars_m2]))

fit_mci <- function(train = rep(TRUE, n_exist)) {
  objective <- function(p) {
    T_hat <- predict_totals(D_exist, X_exist %*% p[-1], p[1])
    log_loss(T_hat[train], T_obs[train])
  }
  optim(c(-2, rep(0, length(vars_m2))), objective,
        method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE, control = list(maxit = 500))
}

coef_table <- function(fit, n_obs) {
  sigma2 <- fit$value / (n_obs - length(fit$par))
  se     <- sqrt(diag(2 * sigma2 * solve(fit$hessian)))
  tibble(term      = c("lambda (distance)", vars_m2),
         estimate  = fit$par,
         std_error = se,
         z         = fit$par / se,
         p_value   = 2 * pnorm(-abs(fit$par / se)))
}

m2 <- fit_mci()
m2$convergence   # 0 means the search converged
```

The interpretation of the estimates is as follows:

- **Distance decay** ($\lambda$ = -2.52) remains steeper than -2 once station attributes are accounted for. Its 95% confidence interval, -2.74 to -2.29, excludes -2.
- **Number of lines** (`n_lines`) has a strong positive effect. An exponent of 1.16 means a two-line interchange is about 2.2 times as attractive as an otherwise similar single-line station. Residents will travel further to an interchange because it reaches more destinations without a transfer.
- **MRT versus LRT** (`mrt`) is strongly significant. Holding other attributes equal, an LRT station is only about 4% as attractive as an MRT station.
- **Bus stops within 400 m** (`bus_stops`) has a positive effect. Stations well served by feeder buses draw residents from further away, consistent with the importance of public transport access in Zhu et al. (2021).
- **Shopping and food** (`shopping`, `food`) should be read together. `shopping` has a positive exponent (0.31) and `food` a small negative one (-0.16). ### 5.8 Holdout Validation: Predicting Recently Opened Stations

## 6. Predicting Ridership at the JRL and CRL Stations

### 6.1 Predicted Ridership and Sensitivity to Distance Decay

The calibrated M2 parameters are applied to the future network of 213 stations. The attractiveness of the new stations is computed from their own attributes (Section 4.9), with the same exponents as the existing stations. Market potential is held at its June 2026 level.

To show how sensitive the predictions are to distance decay, the most influential parameter, the predictions are repeated with $\lambda$ shifted by 0.5 in each direction while the attractiveness exponents are kept fixed. A **steeper** decay ($\lambda - 0.5$) means residents keep more strongly to their nearest station. A **flatter** decay ($\lambda + 0.5$) means they are more willing to travel further to a more attractive station. The two are alternative assumptions rather than lower and upper bounds: a steeper decay raises the prediction for some stations and lowers it for others.

As a benchmark for "low ridership", the lower quartile of observed morning-peak tap-ins at existing MRT stations is used. A new station predicted below this level would be among the least-used quarter of MRT stations even after travel habits have adjusted.

### 6.2 Impact on the Ridership of Existing Stations

To isolate the effect of the new lines, the M2 model is run twice with the same parameters and the same population: once with the existing network and once with the future network. The difference for each existing station is therefore due only to the new stations. Errors in the model affect both runs and largely cancel.

The predicted percentage change is then applied to each station's observed ridership. This gives an expected future ridership that starts from what the station actually carries today, rather than from the model's prediction.

Section 5.7 showed that the model fits some stations poorly, for example the Tuas stations, whose riders are mostly non-residents. A predicted change at such a station is unreliable, because the model does not represent who actually uses it. Stations whose predicted ridership in Section 5.7 was within a factor of two of observed ridership (a ratio between 0.5 and 2) are therefore flagged as reliable, and the others as poorly fitted.

The future distance matrix lists the existing stations first, in the same order as the existing network, so the two sets of predictions can be compared position by position. This is checked with *stopifnot()*.


::: {.cell}

The two largest losses need caution. Joo Koon (-66.8%) and Gul Circle (-62.5%), the outlier in the 3-5 km band. Beyond 5 km, the median change does not reach zero but stays at about -6.1%. This is a property of the model rather than a real effect, and it has two causes:

1. **The total number of trips is held constant.** The 12.1% of trips taken by the new stations must therefore come from existing ones.
2. **New options draw proportionally from all stations.** In the Huff and MCI models, a new alternative takes its share proportionally from every station a resident might use, however unlikely. This is the independence-of-irrelevant-alternatives property of these models. So a resident in Jurong who switches to a JRL station slightly reduces the predicted ridership of every station in the network, including those in the CBD.

The background loss of about 6% should therefore be read as the baseline. Only losses well beyond it reflect genuine local competition.

#### 6.2.4 Checking an alternative choice set

One way to remove the background loss would be to restrict each resident's choice to stations within a cutoff distance, so that distant stations are not affected at all. To test this alternative, M2 is recalibrated with stations beyond 3 km and 5 km excluded from each resident's choice set. Each resident's nearest station is always kept, so that every hexagon has at least one option.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
huff_prob_cut <- function(D, logA, lambda, cutoff) {
  U <- sweep(lambda * log(D), 2, logA, "+")
  U[D > pmax(cutoff, apply(D, 1, min))] <- -Inf   # exclude stations beyond the cutoff
  U <- U - apply(U, 1, max)
  P <- exp(U)
  P / rowSums(P)
}

choice_set_check <- map_dfr(c(5000, 3000), \(cutoff) {
  totals <- function(p) as.vector(crossprod(
    huff_prob_cut(D_exist, X_exist %*% p[-1], p[1], cutoff), C_i * trip_rate))
  fit <- optim(c(-2, rep(0, length(vars_m2))),
               \(p) log_loss(pmax(totals(p), 1e-6), T_obs),
               method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 500))
  T_hat <- totals(fit$par)
  tibble(choice_set           = paste("Stations within", cutoff / 1000, "km"),
         lambda               = fit$par[1],
         pseudo_r2            = cor(T_hat, T_obs)^2,
         r2_log               = cor(log(pmax(T_hat, 1e-6)), log(T_obs))^2,
         stations_with_no_riders = sum(T_hat < 1))
})

bind_rows(fit_stats(T_m2, T_obs) %>%
            transmute(choice_set = "All stations (M2)", lambda = lambda_m2,
                      pseudo_r2, r2_log, stations_with_no_riders = sum(T_m2 < 1)),
          choice_set_check) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) %>%
  kable()
```

### 6.4 Summary of Findings

**Objective 1: calibrating the model.** The MCI model explains most of the variation in morning-peak tap-ins at existing stations (pseudo-R² of 0.83, against 0.53 for distance alone). Residents strongly prefer nearby stations ($\lambda$ = -2.52). Beyond distance, the attributes that matter are the number of lines, MRT rather than LRT service, feeder bus access and, to a lesser extent, shopping around the station.

**Objective 2: predicting ridership at the new stations.** The 29 new stations are predicted to carry 12.1% of morning-peak tap-ins. Stations in established housing areas, such as Serangoon North, Pasir Ris East and Choa Chu Kang West, are predicted to be the busiest. Nine stations are predicted below the ridership of the least-used quarter of existing MRT stations. Most of them serve the NTU campus, industrial estates or the future airport area, where demand comes from destinations and non-residents that this model does not capture. The holdout test suggests ridership in the opening years will be lower than predicted.

**Objective 3: impact on existing stations.** The impact is concentrated along the new lines and fades within about 3 km. The largest losses are on the East-West Line between Jurong East and Joo Koon and on the North-South Line around Bukit Batok. Among the interchanges that gain a line, the CRL interchanges at Hougang, Ang Mo Kio and Bright Hill gain riders. The JRL interchanges at Boon Lay, Jurong East and Choa Chu Kang lose tap-ins, but they will carry new transfer traffic that tap-ins do not measure. Beyond the new corridors, the predicted changes reflect a small background loss that comes from the model's structure rather than real competition.

## 7. Value-Added Analysis: Change in Access to MRT/LRT

Sections 5 and 6 view the new lines from the stations' side: how many riders each station gains or loses. This section views them from the residents' side: how much rail service each hexagon can reach, after accounting for the other residents competing for the same stations. This links the exercise to urban sustainability, as it shows which communities gain access to rail and whether the new lines reach areas that were poorly served. It also relates to the government's target of 8 in 10 households being within a 10-minute walk of a train station by the 2030s (Ministry of Transport, 2024).

### 7.1 Method

Access is measured with the two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) method (Luo & Wang, 2003). Each station's supply is first divided among the residents within its catchment. Each hexagon's accessibility is then the sum of the shares of the stations it can reach.

The original method counts a resident in full at every station within reach. Where catchments overlap, which is common in Singapore (Section 6.3.3), this counts the same residents several times and understates each station's supply per resident. Luo (2014) addresses this by sharing each resident's demand among the reachable stations using Huff probabilities. The same approach is used here, with the probabilities from the calibrated M2 model (Section 5.5). For hexagon $i$ and station $j$, with catchment distance $d_0$:

$$
P^*_{ij} = \frac{P_{ij}}{\sum_{k:\, d_{ik} \le d_0} P_{ik}} \quad \text{for } d_{ij} \le d_0
$$

$$
R_j = \frac{S_j}{\sum_{i:\, d_{ij} \le d_0} P^*_{ij}\, C_i}, \qquad
A_i = \sum_{j:\, d_{ij} \le d_0} P^*_{ij}\, R_j
$$

$P^*_{ij}$ is the Huff probability rescaled so that it sums to 1 across the stations a resident can reach. $R_j$ is station $j$'s supply per expected user (step 1). $A_i$ is the accessibility of hexagon $i$ (step 2). A hexagon with no station within $d_0$ has an accessibility of 0.

| Component | Choice | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Supply $S_j$ | Number of lines at the station (`n_lines`) | In 2SFCA, supply is a capacity measure (Luo & Wang, 2003), and each line adds trains and seats. Service frequency and train capacity are not available. |
| Demand $C_i$ | Residents aged 15-64 in each hexagon | The same market potential as in the model (Section 4.7) |
| Selection probability $P_{ij}$ | M2 Huff probabilities | Shares each resident's demand among reachable stations (Luo, 2014) |
| Catchment $d_0$ | 800 m, with 1 km as a sensitivity check | About a 10-minute walk, the basis of the government's target. In a Singapore survey, about 60% of MRT passengers walked to their station, over 608 m on average (Olszewski & Wibowo, 2005). |

The 800 m catchment differs from the 400 m radius used for the attractiveness variables in Section 4.9. That radius describes what lies immediately around a station, whereas the catchment describes how far residents are willing to walk to it.

Two caveats apply. First, distances are straight-line. Olszewski and Wibowo (2005) found that the effort of walking to Singapore stations is 20% to 39% greater than the straight-line distance suggests, so an 800 m straight-line catchment corresponds to somewhat more than a 10-minute walk. The coverage figures below should therefore be read as an upper bound. Second, an LRT line counts the same as an MRT line, although LRT trains carry far fewer passengers.

Accessibility is expressed in rail lines per 100,000 residents aged 15-64.

### 7.2 Computing Accessibility

::: callout-note
### AI Use Disclosure

AI tools were used to adapt the Huff-based two-step floating catchment area method to the station network and to draft the R function *fca_access()* and the code that summarises and maps the results. The output was reviewed and run by the author to verify correctness against the study data.
:::

*fca_access()* implements the two steps with matrices, as in Section 5.2. The distance matrices `D_exist` and `D_future` and the probability matrices `P_now` and `P_future` from Section 6.3 have one row per hexagon and one column per station, in the same order, so the function can be applied to both networks unchanged.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fca_access <- function(P, D, supply, cutoff) {
  W <- P * (D <= cutoff)            # Huff probabilities, kept only for stations within the cutoff
  W <- W / rowSums(W)               # rescaled to sum to 1 across the reachable stations
  W[is.na(W)] <- 0                  # hexagons with no station within the cutoff
  demand <- as.vector(crossprod(W, C_i))             # step 1: residents expected at each station
  ratio  <- if_else(demand > 0, supply / demand, 0)  # lines per resident at each station
  as.vector(W %*% ratio)                             # step 2: accessibility of each hexagon
}

cutoff <- 800

access <- tibble(hex_id = hex_ids,
                 pop    = C_i,
                 before = fca_access(P_now,    D_exist,  dest_df$n_lines,        cutoff) * 1e5,
                 after  = fca_access(P_future, D_future, dest_future_df$n_lines, cutoff) * 1e5) %>%
  mutate(change = after - before)
```
:::


Because each resident's probabilities sum to 1, every line within reach of at least one resident is shared out in full. Accessibility weighted by population should therefore add up to the number of lines reached, which is checked below.

## 8. Limitations

The results should be read with the following limitations in mind. Most have been noted where they arise. They are brought together here, grouped by what they affect.

### 8.1 Who is modelled

- **Residents only.** The SingStat population covers citizens and permanent residents. Foreign workers in dormitories, students in campus hostels and cross-border commuters are not included. This explains why the Tuas stations and Kranji are strongly under-predicted (Section 5.7), and why new stations serving industrial estates and the university campus are likely to be under-predicted (Section 6.1).
- **Population is held at June 2026.** New housing completed after this date, notably in Tengah and the future Jurong Lake District, is not included, so predictions for stations in these areas are conservative.
- **Locating residents.** The 51 HDB blocks completed in 2026 are not yet in the building layer (Section 4.7.2). Private-housing residents are spread by land area, so condominiums are weighted the same per square metre as landed housing, and large residential parcels that are not yet developed receive residents in proportion to their size (Section 4.7.4). 3,640 private-housing residents could not be placed. All of these effects are confined within a subzone, as each subzone's total is fixed.

### 8.2 What is measured

- **Morning tap-ins only.** Tap-ins measure where trips start. They miss a station's role as a destination, which is why destination stations such as Expo and Keppel are over-predicted. They also miss transfers between lines, so the predicted losses at the JRL interchanges do not mean fewer passengers pass through them (Section 6.2.2).
- **A short observation period.** Ridership is averaged over three months. For the Circle Line Stage 6 stations, which were still building up ridership, only September is used.

### 8.3 How the model works

- **Calibration from station totals.** Origin-to-station flows are not available, so the model is calibrated on station totals: 184 observations for 10 parameters (Section 5.1.1). The standard errors are approximate, and strongly correlated variables, such as `shopping` and `food`, cannot be fully separated (Section 5.5).
- **Independence of irrelevant alternatives.** A new station draws riders proportionally from every station, producing a background loss of about 6.1% at stations far from the new lines (Section 6.2.3). Only losses well beyond this level should be read as genuine competition.
- **Straight-line distance.** Walking routes, barriers such as expressways and feeder bus services are not modelled. Actual walking effort in Singapore is 20% to 39% greater than straight-line distance suggests (Olszewski & Wibowo, 2005).
- **Immediate adjustment.** The model assumes residents switch to a more attractive station at once. The holdout test shows that recently opened stations are over-predicted by a median factor of 1.7 (Section 5.8), so the predictions describe ridership after travel habits have adjusted.
- **Areal units.** Results may change with the size of the hexagons (the modifiable areal unit problem). The 500 m cell size is finer than station spacing, but was not varied.
- **Points of interest.** OpenStreetMap coverage varies between areas, which affects the attractiveness variables.
- **Accessibility measure.** The 2SFCA analysis uses the number of lines as supply, so an LRT line counts the same as an MRT line, and service frequency is not represented (Section 7.1).

## 9. Conclusion and Recommendations

### 9.1 Conclusion

This exercise calibrated a probabilistic spatial interaction model of station choice for Singapore's MRT and LRT network and used it to assess the Jurong Region Line and Cross Island Line Phase 1.

**RQ1: How well does the model explain ridership, and what matters beyond distance?** The MCI model explains most of the variation in weekday morning-peak tap-ins at the 184 existing stations (pseudo-R² of 0.83, against 0.53 for distance alone). Residents strongly prefer nearby stations ($\lambda$ = -2.52, steeper than the conventional -2). Beyond distance, the number of lines, MRT rather than LRT service and feeder bus access make a station more attractive. The model's largest errors point to riders it does not represent: non-resident workers and passengers arriving at destinations.

**RQ2: What ridership can the new stations expect?** The 29 new stations are predicted to carry 12.1% of morning-peak tap-ins once travel habits have adjusted. Stations in established housing areas, such as Serangoon North, Pasir Ris East and Choa Chu Kang West, are predicted to be the busiest. 9 stations are predicted below the lower quartile of existing MRT stations. Most of them serve industrial estates, the university campus or the airport area, where demand from workers and students is not captured by a residential model.

**RQ3: How will the new lines affect existing stations and market areas?** The impact is local. The largest losses are at East-West Line stations between Jurong East and Joo Koon and around Bukit Batok, and the effect fades within about 3 km of the new lines. The CRL interchanges at Bright Hill, Hougang and Ang Mo Kio gain riders, while the JRL interchanges lose tap-ins but will carry transfer traffic. 147 hexagons change their most likely station.

**Access to rail.** The share of residents aged 15–64 within 800 m of a station rises from 71.6% to 79.7%, with the largest gains in Tengah, Jurong East, Jurong West and Pasir Ris, areas that are currently among the least served.

### 9.2 Recommendations

1. **Treat low predictions as a prompt for further data, not as a verdict.** Before decisions on the timing of opening or service levels at the 9 low-ridership stations, their demand should be estimated with employment, student and dormitory populations, which this model does not include.
2. **Plan for a ramp-up period.** Based on the holdout test, ridership in the first months after opening may be well below the predictions. Service levels can be phased in and adjusted as observed ridership builds up.
3. **Review feeder bus services around the stations that lose riders.** East-West Line stations between Jurong East and Joo Koon are predicted to lose a large share of their morning tap-ins to the JRL. Feeder services into these stations can be reviewed as residents switch to stations nearer home.
4. **Prepare the interchanges for transfer traffic.** Bright Hill and Hougang are predicted to gain substantially in tap-ins, while Boon Lay, Jurong East and Choa Chu Kang will carry transfers between the JRL and the existing lines. Platform and concourse capacity at these stations should account for both.

### 9.3 Future Work

- Calibrate with origin-level data, such as anonymised fare-card records linked to home locations, so that the standard MCI estimation on market shares can be used.
- Add employment and student populations as a second source of demand, and model the evening peak to capture the destination role of stations.
- Replace straight-line distance with walking-network distance, and include feeder bus access time.
- Use projected population for the opening years of the JRL and CRL rather than current population.
- Test the sensitivity of the results to the hexagon size.
